title: Photography direction for a developer-tool company
excerpt: Photograph the real screen of the tool. A slogan about empowering developers, and the stock photos that decorate it, do not belong in the argument.
alt: A workshop where one person points at colorful sticky notes while others sit with laptops. The article is about pointing at the work, not at a slogan on the wall.
caption: The useful gesture is someone pointing at the work itself. Photograph via Unsplash.

faqs.question: What should pictures on a developer-tool site show?
faqs.answer: Show a real screen, transcript, or diff that contains the mechanism. Write the claim first, then choose a frame that a reader could falsify. Meetup photos and neon keyboards show that you have seen an engineer. They do not show that the tool works.

faqs.question: Can you redraw the interface for the marketing site?
faqs.answer: Crop and simplify sample data, and do not invent a layout the product does not ship. This reader will compare the frame to the build they install. A cleaner fiction reads as a mismatch, or as a reason not to trust the rest of the page.

faqs.question: How should alt text describe a product capture?
faqs.answer: State what is in the frame, such as a pull request comment that names a specific failure. Keep secrets out of the alt text and the caption. A slogan is not a description of the picture.

markdown:
Treat developer-tool company website photography as evidence. The frames should show a real screen of the tool. An engineer who is skeptical of marketing treats the picture as a claim. A terminal, a pull request, a trace, or a diff can support that claim. A slogan about empowering developers cannot, and neither can a photograph that exists to decorate the slogan. The frame is part of the argument. If it does not show the mechanism, it is in the way.

Choose fewer pictures. Write the sentence each one must prove. Reject the rest. A short page with one honest capture will outlast a polished page of borrowed offices and hoodies.

## The frame is a claim you can falsify

Before you pick a photograph, write the claim in a sentence an engineer could test. "The review comment names the migration that locks the table." "The trace shows the query under the slow route." Then select or capture a frame that contains exactly that. If you cannot point at the evidence in the pixels, the claim is a caption looking for a different picture.

Do not ask a mood to do this work. Focused. Modern. Human. Those words produce the same stock library for every tool company. The reader has seen the library. They are looking for the line of type that only your tool would render. Give them that line at a size they can read without squinting.

One claim per frame. A hero that includes the team, the city, the laptop, and a hint of the UI shows none of them well. Put the UI in the hero. The city was never the product. The team can appear on the about page, next to responsibilities, where a portrait has a job.

Place a sentence next to the picture that matches the pixels. A caption that upgrades a simple warning into a revolution is the slogan again. Keep the caption as plain as a docstring. The reader should be able to glance from words to screen and agree.

## Photograph the real interface

Capture the tool you ship. Sample data is fine. A redrawn "cleaner" interface is not. This buyer compares your marketing frame to the build they will install. If the spacing, the theme, or the information differ, they will believe the marketing and then feel misled, or they will not believe it and never install. Both outcomes are worse than an ordinary true screenshot.

Crop to the mechanism. The comment, the flag, the plan, the error. Extra browser chrome can go if you are honest about the crop. A new layout that the product does not have cannot. Removing distraction is editing. Inventing a dashboard is fiction.

For a CLI, show a real transcript. The command, the relevant output, a short prompt. Do not typeset a fantasy shell with gradients behind it unless the command is still copy-paste accurate. Accuracy is the aesthetic they respect. You can set the transcript in your brand type. You cannot change the flags.

For a library, a short snippet and its result can be the "photograph." Treat it with the same discipline. Real API. Real result. No pseudo-code that almost matches. If the snippet is the artifact, it does not need a stock desk under it. Let it sit on a quiet ground so the code is the picture.

Got Next and Leadly, public product interfaces, show how a screen can be about one job. Borrow that restraint when you frame a developer tool. The action in the frame should be countable on one hand. A screen with twenty equal panels photographs as noise, which may mean the product needs an edit before the site does.

## Reject the slogan and the pictures that serve it

Reject "empowering developers" as a headline, and reject the photos commissioned to match it. Raised hands at a meetup. A hoodie in profile. A neon keyboard. Those frames argue that you have seen a developer. They do not argue that the tool works. This reader does not need to be depicted. They need the output.

Reject a feature grid as an illustration. Six abstract icons with soft names are the slogan broken into tiles. A custom illustration of the same grid is still the grid. Spend the space on one true screen. If you have six capabilities, choose the one the homepage is for. The others can be sentences under docs headings.

Reject charts nobody can read, photographed at an angle so the numbers strobe. Angle and glare are how a real screen becomes a texture. If a camera cannot hold the UI steady, use a direct capture and compose it in the layout. You are not making a movie poster. You are showing a tool.

Reject customer screens you are not allowed to show. Rebuild the situation with sample data and say so in the caption if the context could be mistaken for a private incident. A labeled sample is a claim. A leaked dashboard is a different kind of reputation.

## A brief for the person making the frames

Write one page. The claim. The exact screen or command. What must be legible. What must not appear. The crop for the phone, which will not be the same as the wide crop. The sentence that will sit beside the frame, so nobody is guessing at a mood board.

Ask for a direct capture first. Add a photographed scene only if the scene helps the claim, such as a CI log on a laptop where the log is still readable. If the scene wins and the log loses, throw the frame away. You can reshoot a desk. You cannot recover an unreadable error.

Review selects against the claim, in writing. "Shows the lock, names the file, does not offer the suppression we refused." If a select is only "nice light," it is not a select for this page. Nice light can exist in the margins of a portrait. It does not get the hero.

Keep the product's real theme. Do not recolor a dark tool into a peach brand world because the marketing site is warm. The mismatch reads as two products. A quiet marketing page can frame a dense tool without repainting it. Density is sometimes the point. A trading interface such as the public Trade Moai concept is a reminder that the job decides how much information belongs in the frame. A developer tool deserves the same honesty. Do not thin the evidence into a lifestyle crop.

## Alt text, captions, and honesty

The W3C WCAG overview includes text alternatives so a person who does not see the image still gets the content. Write the alt as what is in the frame. "A pull request comment that names a migration locking a table." Do not stuff a slogan into the alt. Do not write "developer empowerment image." The alt is a technical caption for someone who needs it.

The visible caption can carry the claim in one sentence, including a credit line your process requires. Keep secrets out of both. If you blurred a token, do not repeat the token in the caption. If the data is a sample, the caption can say "sample project" so a careful reader does not think you exposed a customer.

Captions are also where you prevent the picture from drifting back into advertising. Read the caption aloud. If it could sit under a stock photo of a laptop, it is not specific enough. Name the object the tool touched.

Use the same frames across the site so the tool looks like one tool. A new metaphorical photo in every section feels like a theme week. Reuse the review comment, the trace, the install transcript. Repetition of a true artifact builds memory. Repetition of stock builds nothing.

## Where pictures help, and where they do not

The first view gets the real screen. A later section can show a second step of the same job. The about page can show a person who maintains it. Pricing usually needs no mood at all. A picture next to a price should be the limit in the product, or it should be absent.

Do not drop a full-bleed office photo between the install command and the explanation of the flag. That photo is an interruption in a procedure. Procedures want sequence and type. If you want warmth, use space and a consistent caption style. Warmth is not the same as a rented interior.

Illustrations can explain a flow when a screenshot cannot show time. Keep them as plain as a diagram. Boxes, arrows, the objects from the tool. An illustrated mascot pointing at abstract shapes is the slogan with a face. Skip it unless the mascot is truly how the docs teach, and even then, do not let it occupy the hero.

When a frame is almost right, fix the product capture rather than compensating with a caption. A caption can name a line. It cannot invent legibility. If the warning is too small, recrop. If the sample data is cute instead of plausible, replace the data. Plausible sample data looks boring, which is what a production tool looks like. Cute data looks like a demo that will not survive contact with a repository. Choose boring.

The frame has to survive a phone, because that is where a skeptical reader often takes the first look. A wide screenshot that shrinks to dust has lost the claim. Read [how the mobile visit should still show a real screen and a way to try](/blog/the-mobile-visit-for-a-developer-tool-company) before you approve a crop that only works on a large monitor.

To see screens treated as the argument, look at [Hanabi's selected work](https://tryhanabi.com/#works). The photograph, or the capture, should be something a stranger could learn from.
